cues.text: Who Is Like God?
The name Michael — Hebrew Mî-kāʾēl — is not a statement but a question: who is like God?
Christian tradition has long heard the whole of this archangel's mission summed up in that very name, in just four words.
It is not self-assertion, but a fierce, humbling challenge thrown back at any power, however great, that would set itself up as God's rival.
Of the countless angels described in Scripture, only three are ever named outright, and Michael is named first among them — called, in the Book of Daniel, one of the chief princes .
The Church has honored him ever since as the captain of the heavenly host, the foremost of the nine angelic choirs in rank if not always in the theologians' precise ordering of them.
Prince of Daniel's People
Michael's first scriptural appearances come in the Book of Daniel, where he is shown as the great guardian and advocate of Israel against hostile earthly powers.
When the angel sent to Daniel is delayed three weeks by the prince of the kingdom of Persia , it is Michael who comes to his aid.
Scripture describes him as one of the chief princes who alone stands with him against the opposition (Daniel 10:13).

Later in the same book, at the close of a vision concerning the last days, Daniel is told plainly: at that time shall Michael rise up, the great prince, who standeth for the children of thy people (Daniel 12:1).
He is a guardian appointed not for one crisis only, but for the whole span of his people's trial, until the very end of the age.
War in Heaven
The Book of Revelation carries Michael's role to its cosmic conclusion.
In a vision of the Church's final struggle, John sees war in heaven: Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon, and the dragon fought and his angels .
The ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan , is thrown down, defeated (Revelation 12:7–9).
Some later Christian reflection has connected this same vision's woman clothed with the sun , threatened by the dragon, to the Blessed Virgin Mary and to the Church she images.

Read this way, Michael's victory becomes not a distant episode, but the pledge of protection extended to Mary's own spiritual children, the whole company of believers the dragon still seeks to devour.
Contending for the Body of Moses
A single, striking verse in the Epistle of St.
Jude shows Michael in a very different register: not the commander of armies but a careful, restrained officer of heaven's own justice.
Disputing with the devil about the body of Moses , Jude tells us, Michael durst not bring against him a railing judgment, but said: The Lord command thee (Jude 1:9).
Even at the height of his power, Michael does not presume to condemn on his own authority — he defers entirely to the judgment of God.
The Church has long read in this brief scene a lesson as important as any of his battles: that true strength submits itself to a higher authority rather than exercising judgment on its own account.
Guardian of the Church and of Every Soul
Beyond these named scriptural appearances, a venerable tradition has honored Michael as guardian not only of Israel, but of the Church that succeeded it.
He is also honored as the angel who comes to each soul at the hour of death, to defend it in its final trial and present it before God's judgment.
Pope Leo XIII is recorded by later accounts to have experienced, in 1884, a vision of the powers of darkness gathering against the Church.
Whatever its precise details, the vision moved him to compose the prayer beginning Saint Michael the Archangel, defend us in battle , ordering it recited after every low Mass.
That practice lapsed after Vatican II, though Popes John Paul II and Francis both later urged the faithful to take it up again.
Legacy

Feast kept, since the 1969 calendar reform, together with Gabriel and Raphael on 29 September , Michael remains patron of soldiers, police officers, and all who stand watch against danger on others' behalf.
He is also patron of the dying, for whom the Church has always asked his presence at the last and hardest hour.
We recognize in Michael something every believer eventually needs: not a power that fights on our behalf instead of us, but a companion in the one battle none of us can finally avoid.
That battle is the ancient contest between good and evil that Christ has already, decisively, won, and into which Michael's own cry still summons every soul willing to ask, with him, who is like God?
